## Lithosphere plates and what drives their motion
The lithosphere is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates that float on the ductile asthenosphere. Think of it like a competitive baking show: firm, set layers of a tiered cake resting on a soft, yielding filling beneath. The plates move because of mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push, and their relative motion is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
Plate boundaries come in three types, each with its own seismic style. Divergent boundaries: plates pull apart, producing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Convergent boundaries: plates collide, producing thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. Transform boundaries: plates slide past one another, producing strike-slip earthquakes from shallow to intermediate depths.
Earthquakes cluster at boundaries for four reasons. First, stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, and strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Second, fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip. Third, rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation. Fourth, geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
The key point: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. Many people assume quakes occur anywhere at random; the material says otherwise — their pattern maps the plate interactions themselves. Keep this single point in mind for tomorrow: the earthquake map is the plate-interaction map.

## Why Earthquakes Cluster at Boundaries
The lithosphere is the rigid outer layer of Earth. It is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates that float on the ductile asthenosphere. The asthenosphere is ductile, meaning it flows slowly instead of breaking.
Plates move because of mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push. Their relative motion is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹). Think of it like crypto trading: each position changes slowly, a few percent per day, yet over months the total shift is large.
There are three boundary types. Divergent: plates pull apart, giving normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Convergent: plates collide, giving thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. Transform: plates slide past, giving strike-slip earthquakes from shallow to intermediate.
Why do earthquakes cluster at edges? First, stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Think of it like a marching band holding a formation under pressure: the push builds until someone breaks rank. Second, fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip.
Third, rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation there. Fourth, geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
Key point: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. In other words, the map of earthquakes shows where and how plates move against each other.
